steps.html:
Graffiti, then broken windows, twice in one month. Three people work out what to do about it, reject two solutions and settle on two others in under three minutes. Then a film about where boredom came from, and what it is for.

  • Follow a problem being solved in real time
  • Propose a solution and say why another will not work
  • Watch a documentary about boredom
  • Write an article giving advice

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: Compare: 'One alternative would be to install cameras' and 'Would it be worth putting in fake cameras?'
steps.prompt: Why does one take the infinitive and the other -ing?
options: Would be to is followed by an infinitive; worth is followed by -ing.
The first is a question and the second is a statement.
steps.answer: Would be to is followed by an infinitive; worth is followed by -ing.
steps.why: Worth, point in and no harm in all take -ing. Would be to and need to take the infinitive.

steps.title: Which form each advice phrase takes
steps.html:
Recycled from Lessons 33, 34 and 35, and now inside the phrases you use to propose something.

Advice phrases divide neatly, and the division is the same one you already know: anything ending in a preposition takes -ing; anything ending in to as part of an infinitive takes the base form.

+ -ing: it's worth …, there's no point in …, there's no harm in …, I'd suggest …, how about …, what about …, it's a question of …

+ infinitive: one alternative would be to …, a better way forward would be to …, we need to …, the answer is to …, I'd advise you to …, my advice would be to …

Two traps. Suggest never takes an object plus infinitive: I'd suggest installing lights or I suggest that you install lights, never I suggest you to install.

And recommend behaves the same way: I recommend trying it or I recommend that you try it, never I recommend you to try. Advise, on the other hand, does take the object and infinitive: I'd advise you to try it.

steps.title: The same advice, four ways
steps.html:
1. The advice: install movement-sensitive lights.
  2. Tentative, with -ing: Would it be worth putting in some lights? A question, and nobody is committed.
  3. Neutral, with the infinitive: One alternative would be to put in some lights. On the table, not pushed.
  4. Stronger, with -ing: I'd suggest putting in some lights. Note: never I'd suggest you to put in.
  5. Strongest, with object and infinitive: I'd advise you to put in some lights. Advise is the one verb here that takes an object plus infinitive.

steps.title: Write an article giving advice.
steps.sub: 160–190 words. Title: What to do when you are bored at work. Set out the problem, propose two or three solutions, and rule one out.
steps.html:
• Open by correcting a common assumption about the problem.
  • Propose the obvious solution, then say why it is not enough.
  • Rule one thing out, using <i>there is no point in…</i>
  • Propose the better solution, using <i>a better way forward would be to…</i>
  • Close with what the boredom actually means.

Useful language

  • The obvious solution would be to … , but …
  • It is worth …-ing , especially if …
  • There is no point in …-ing , because …
  • A better way forward would be to …
  • I would suggest …-ing rather than …-ing
  • There is no harm in …-ing as well.
steps.modelHtml:
What to do when you are bored at work

Most advice about boredom at work assumes you have too much to do. Often the opposite is true: the problem is a task that takes ten minutes and an afternoon that does not.

The obvious solution would be to ask for more work, and it is worth trying once. But it frequently produces another ten-minute task, and you are back to doing nothing an hour later.

There is no point in pretending to be busy either. It is exhausting, it fools nobody, and it uses the concentration you will need when something real arrives.

A better way forward would be to build something that outlasts the afternoon. Learn the part of the system nobody understands. Write the document your team keeps saying somebody should write. There is no harm in asking permission first, though in my experience nobody refuses.

Boredom at work is a signal, not a punishment. It is usually telling you that the job is smaller than you are.
